lesson.title: The Imaginary Half of Admittance: How Susceptance Adds Up in Parallel
lesson.summary: Susceptance B, the imaginary part of admittance, measures how much an inductor or capacitor contributes to a parallel circuit's total current per volt, and unlike reactance, susceptances of parallel branches add directly.
lesson.body:
Susceptance, symbol B, is the imaginary part of admittance, Y = G + jB, and it measures how strongly an inductor or capacitor contributes to the total current a parallel branch draws for each volt applied. Its sign convention mirrors reactance's but works out inverted: a capacitor contributes a positive susceptance, BC = wC, while an inductor contributes a negative susceptance, BL = -1/(wL). Compare that to reactance, where the capacitor is the negative one, XC = -1/(wC), and the inductor the positive one, XL = wL. The flip happens because susceptance comes from inverting impedance, and inverting a complex number flips the sign of its angle.

The entire reason susceptance earns its own name, rather than just being called out as part of admittance, is how simply it combines in parallel circuits. Reactances of series elements add directly, but reactances of parallel elements do not, you would need the same awkward reciprocal-of-sum formula that plagues parallel resistances. Susceptances sidestep that problem completely: for branches in parallel, Btotal = B1 + B2 + B3 + ..., just as conductances add for parallel resistors. This is the whole payoff of working in admittance and susceptance rather than impedance and reactance whenever a circuit's structure is parallel rather than series.

Consider an inductor and a capacitor connected in parallel, with L = 0.1 H and C = 50 microfarads, driven at w = 1000 rad/s. The inductive susceptance is BL = -1/(wL) = -1/(1000 times 0.1) = -1/100 = -0.01 S. The capacitive susceptance is BC = wC = 1000 times 50e-6 = 0.05 S. Adding them directly gives Btotal = BC + BL = 0.05 - 0.01 = 0.04 S, a net positive, capacitive susceptance. It is worth checking where these two would exactly cancel: setting BL = -BC gives 1/(wL) = wC, so w0 = 1/sqrt(LC) = 1/sqrt(0.1 times 50e-6) = 1/sqrt(5e-6), about 447.2 rad/s. Since our operating frequency, 1000 rad/s, is well above that resonant value, the capacitor dominates, which is exactly what the positive net susceptance tells us.

The sign of Btotal is a fast diagnostic for how a parallel combination behaves as a whole: positive means the branch net draws current in the same relative sense a capacitor would, current leading voltage, negative means it behaves inductively, current lagging voltage, and zero means the reactive currents from the inductor and capacitor cancel exactly, leaving only resistive current to flow, the parallel resonance condition. That cancellation matters far beyond circuit theory homework. It is the same underlying idea power engineers exploit when they add capacitor banks to a plant's wiring to offset the inductive susceptance of motors, which is where susceptance reconnects with power factor and reactive power later in this material, once real power and reactive power have been defined in their own right.
